extracted.intended_audience: advanced students and researchers in classical mechanics / mathematical physics (readers of Newton's Principia)
extracted.subtask_description: A collection of propositions, lemmas and problems from Newtonian classical mechanics that determine how distributed (spherical, shell, segmental, circular, or solid) masses attract point-particles or other bodies under various point-force laws (inverse-square, linear, inverse-cube, etc.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corpusculum intra Sphæram attrahitur vi proportionali distantiæ a centro
rubrics_metrics.description: centes in duplicata ratione distantiarum a punctis: dico quod corpusculum intra Sphæram constitutum attrahitur vi proportionali distantiæ suæ ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argument: decompose the enclosing sphere into concentric spherical surfaces; by Theorem XXX the contributions from concentric spherical surfaces exterior to the chosen interior sphere cancel, leaving only the inner sphere whose attraction is proportional to the distance PS. (See Scholium about interpreting surfaces/points as infinitely thin rings/particles.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXIV / Theor. XXXIV — Exterior attraction inverse-square
rubrics_metrics.description: Iisdem positis, dico quod corpusculum extra Sphæram constitutum attrahitur vi reciproce proportionali quadrato distantiæ suæ ab ipsius centro.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the sphere into innumerable concentric spherical surfaces; each surface's attraction on the external point is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from that surface to the point (per Theorem XXXI); summing these gives that the whole sphere attracts as if its mass were concentrated at its center (proof Q.E.D.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 1 to LXXIV — equal-distance rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Hinc in æqualibus distantiis a centris homogenearum Sphærarum, attractiones sunt ut Sphæræ.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If distances from centers are proportional to diameters, then forces are proportional to diameters; adjusting distance to make them equal yields attraction proportional to the spheres themselves (i.e., mass).

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 2 to LXXIV — attraction proportional to sphere × inverse-square distance
rubrics_metrics.description: In distantiis quibusvis attractiones sunt ut Sphæræ applicatæ ad quadrata distantiarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: General statement: attraction between homogeneous spheres is proportional to their content (volume/mass) and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between centers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corol. 3 to LXXIV — implication for particulate laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpusculum extra Sphæram homogeneam positum trahitur vi reciproce proportionali quadrato distantiæ suæ ab ipsius centro, constet autem Sphæra ex particulis attractivis; decrescet vis particulæ cujusq; in duplicata ratione distantiæ a particula.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a homogeneous sphere exerts inverse-square attraction externally and the sphere is composed of attractive particles, then each particle's attractive strength must itself decrease as the inverse-square of distance from that particle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXV / Theor. XXXV — inverse-square point-law implies sphere–sphere inverse-square
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad Sphæræ datæ puncta singula tendant vires æquales centripetæ decrescentes in duplicata ratione distantiarum a punctis, dico quod Sphæra quævis alia similaris attrahitur vi reciproce proportionalis quadrato distantiæ centrorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If at each point of a sphere there is a centripetal force on a distant body that decreases inverse-square with distance, then a similar sphere is attracted as if all mass were at its center — inverse-square dependence between centers. Proof uses equivalence with a single central particle (Theorem XXXIV).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXVI / Theor. XXXVI — radially varying spheres but inverse-square total
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Sphæræ in progressu a centro ad circumferentiam ... dissimilares, ... & vis attractiva puncti cujusq; decrescit in duplicata ratione distantiæ corporis attracti: dico quod vis tota qua hujusmodi Sphæra una attrahit aliam sit reciproce proportionalis quadrato distantiæ centrorum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when spheres have radial variation in density and point-attractive strength, provided they are similar around any given radius (i.e., angularly similar at each radius) and point-attractions decay inverse-square, the total mutual attraction of such composite spheres remains inverse-square between centers (argument by decomposing into concentric shells and summing). Corollaries give consequences for periods and proportionalities of rotating spheres.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXVII / Theor. XXXVII — linear point-law gives linear center–center force
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad singula Sphærarum puncta tendant vires centripetæ proportionales distantiis punctorum a corporibus attractis: dico quod vis composita, qua Sphæræ duæ se mutuo trahent, est ut distantia inter centra Sphærarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each point of a sphere exerts a centripetal force proportional to the distance to the attracted body (i.e., a linear force law), then two similar spheres attract each other with a force proportional to the distance between their centers. Multiple 'cases' (1–6) show computations for interior/exterior placements and composition arguments reducing to single-center equivalents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXVIII / Theor. XXXVIII — dissimilar radial spheres with linear point-law
rubrics_metrics.description: Si Sphæræ in progressu a centro ad circumferentiam sint utcunq; dissimilares & inæquabiles, in progressu vero per circuitum ad datam omnem a centro distantiam sint undiq; similares; & vis attractiva puncti cujusq; sit ut distantia corporis attracti: dico quod vis tota qua hujusmodi Sphæræ duæ se mutuo trahunt sit proportionalis distantiæ inter centra Sphærarum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogous to LXXVI but for the linear (proportional-to-distance) point-force law: despite radial differences, similarity at each radius ensures total attraction is proportional to center-to-center distance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scholium on notable cases — inverse-square and linear give conic motion
rubrics_metrics.description: Attractionum Casus duos insigniores jam dedi expositos; nimirum ubi vires centripetæ decrescunt in duplicata distantiarum ratione, vel crescunt in distantiarum ratione simplici; efficientes in utroq; Casu ut corpora gyrentur in Conicis Sectionibus...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observation: the two important point-force laws are inverse-square and linear (proportional to distance); both lead to motion in conic sections (ellipses, etc.) for bodies moving under such central forces. The text prefers a general method to encompass other less-elegant cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma XXIX — limiting ratio for vanishing arcs and lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Si describantur centro S circulus quilibet AEB, & centro P circuli duo EF, ef, secantes priorem in E, e, lineamq; PS in F, f; & ad PS demittantur perpendicula ED, ed: dico quod si distantia arcuum EF, ef in infinitum minui intelligatur, ratio ultima lineæ evanescentis Dd ad lineam evanescentem Ff ea sit, quæ lineæ PE ad lineam PS.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical lemma giving limiting proportionality relationships used in converting infinitesimal surface/arc elements to linear elements in subsequent area/force computations (used in Theorem XXXIX onward).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXIX / Theor. XXXIX — thin revolving surface element force composition
rubrics_metrics.description: Si superficies ob latitudinem infinite diminutam jamjam evanescens EFfe, convolutione sui circa axem PS, describat solidum Sphæricum concavo-convexum, ad cujus particulas singulas æquales tendant æquales vires centripetæ: dico quod vis, qua solidum illud trahit corpusculum situm in P, est in ratione composita ex ratione solidi DEq. × Ff & ratione vis qua particula data in loco Ff traheret idem corpusculum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: approximate a thin surface by annular elements whose contribution equals DE^2 × Ff (Archimedean result); the force of the thin shell on P is therefore proportional to that product and to the point-force a particle at Ff would exert. This yields a way to integrate surface contributions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXX / Theor. XL — sphere's total attraction as area under axis-curve
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad Sphæræ alicujus AEB, centro S descriptae, particulas singulas æquales tendant æquales vires centripetæ, & ad Sphæræ axem AB, in quo corpusculum aliquod P locatur, erigantur de punctis singulis D perpendicula DE, Sphæræ occurrentia in E, & in ipsis capiantur longitudines DN, quæ sint ut quantitas DEq. × PS ÷ PE & vis quam Sphæræ particula sita in axe ad distantiam PE exercet in corpusculum P conjunctim: dico quod vis tota, qua corpusculum P trahitur versus Sphæram, est ut area comprehensa sub axe Sphæræ AB & linea curva ANB, quam punctum N perpetuo tangit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct DN proportional to DE^2 × PS/PE × (local particle force); summing (integrating) the lamina contributions shows the total attraction equals the area ABNA. Corollaries give special cases where particle-force laws simplify DN and thus the area representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollaries to Prop. LXXX — special power laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Corol.1–4: If particle centripetal force is constant / inversely proportional to distance / inversely proportional to square / inversely proportional to cube, then with appropriate choices for DN (DN = DE^2×PS/PE ÷ PE^k), the total attraction of the whole sphere on P is proportional to the area ABNA (with explicit forms dependent on k).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These corollaries give recipes to set DN (the ordinate) corresponding to several power-law dependences of point-attraction so that sphere's total attraction reduces to computing an area under the axis-curve; used to derive explicit dependence of total force on distances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXI / Prob. XLI — measuring area ABNA; worked examples
rubrics_metrics.description: Stantibus jam positis, mensuranda est Area ABNA. (Construction and algebraic manipulations leading to expressions for DE^2 × PS ÷ (PE × V) resolving into three parts whose areas are computable by known methods.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gives construction to compute area ABNA used in Prop. LXXX. Examples: (1) if point-force ∝ 1/PE (inverse-linear), one gets an explicit construction via hyperbola; (2) if point-force ∝ 1/PE^3 (inverse-cube) or (3) inverse-fourth, explicit formulae and geometric constructions are given. Example 3 yields that when point-force decays as fourth power, total attraction of a center particle is proportional to SI^3/PI (i.e., reciprocal to PS^3×PI).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXII / Theor. XLI — relation of interior and exterior attractions under power laws
rubrics_metrics.description: In Sphæra centro S intervallo SA descripta, si capiantur SI, SA, SP continue proportionales: dico quod corpusculi intra Sphæram in loco quovis I attractio est ad attractionem ipsius extra Sphæram in loco P, in ratione composita ex dimidiata ratione distantiarum a centro IS, PS & dimidiata ratione virium centripetarum, in locis illis P & I, ad centrum tendentium.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the point-force law at sphere particles is a power law of distance D^n, the ratio of attraction at an interior point I to that at an exterior point P combines (half)ratios of distances and (half)ratios of the point-force intensities at those locations. Special cases: for inverse-linear, inverse-square, inverse-cube, etc., explicit interior-vs-exterior relations are derived (e.g., under certain n the attractions can be equal or scale simply).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXIII / Prob. XLII — attraction of a sphere's segment on center
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire vim qua corpusculum in centro Sphæræ locatum ad ejus segmentum quodcunq; attrahitur. ... Ponamus vires attractivas particularum Sphæræ esse reciproce ut distantiarum dignitas illa cujus Index est n; & vis qua superficies FE trahit corpus P erit ut DF × O ÷ PF^(n-1).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides a formula for the force exerted on a central particle by an arbitrary spherical segment (specified by plane and spherical cap), using the small physical depth O and integrating surface annuli; the net force is represented by a curvilinear area obtained by applying ordinates proportional to DF×O/PF^(n-1).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXIV / Prob. XLIII — attraction of a segment on off-center axial point
rubrics_metrics.description: Invenire vim qua corpusculum, extra centrum Sphæræ in axe segmenti cujusvis locatum, attrahitur ab eodem segmento.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Break the spherical cap into two parts by a spherical surface through P and use Prop. LXXXI (center case) and LXXXIII (segment formulas) to compute forces of each part and sum to get the total force for a point on the axis but not at the center.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXV / Theor. XLII (Sect. XIII) — contact amplification when point-law decays faster than inverse-square
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corporis attracti, ubi attrahenti contiguum est, attractio longe fortior sit, quam cum vel minimo intervallo separantur ab invicem: vires particularum trahentis, in recessu corporis attracti, decrescunt in ratione plusquam duplicata distantiarum a particulis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the particulate attractive forces decay faster than inverse-square with separation, then bodies in contact exhibit much stronger attraction than when separated; removing or adding remote parts of bodies does not much change contact attraction. The proposition justifies why contact forces can be much stronger under certain microscopic force laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXVI / Theor. XLIII — strong contact when point-law decays inverse-cube or faster
rubrics_metrics.description: Si particularum, ex quibus corpus attractivum componitur, vires in recessu corporis attracti decrescunt in triplicata vel plusquam triplicata ratione distantiarum a particulis: attractio longe fortior erit in contactu, quam cum attrahens & attractum intervallo vel minimo separantur ab invicem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By the computations of Problem XLI and examples, if point-attractive strength decays as 1/D^3 or faster, the approach to contact leads to arbitrarily large increases in attraction; applicable to concavo-convex shells and general bodies by adding/subtracting remote material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXVII / Theor. XLIV — scaling/composition principle for similar bodies
rubrics_metrics.description: Si corpora duo sibi invicem similia & ex materia æqualiter attractiva constantia seorsim attrahant corpuscula sibi ipsis proportionalia & ad se similiter posita: attractiones acceleratrices corpusculorum in corpora tota erunt ut attractiones acceleratrices corpusculorum in eorum particulas totis proportionales & in totis similiter positas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If bodies are similar and made of the same attractive material, attraction of composite bodies can be deduced by summing (composing) attractions of corresponding particles; corollaries provide explicit proportionalities for bodies whose particle-force law decays as various powers (e.g., inverse-square gives attraction ∝ A^3/A^2 = A, etc.), enabling scaling relations between body sizes and mutual accelerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. LXXXVIII / Theor. XLV — linear point-law yields center-of-gravity equivalence
rubrics_metrics.description: Si particularum æqualium corporis cujuscunq; vires attractivæ sint ut distantiæ locorum a particulis: vis corporis totius tendet ad ipsius centrum gravitatis; & eadem erit cum vi globi ex materia consimili & æquali constantis & centrum habentis in ejus centro gravitatis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If each particle's attractive strength is proportional to its distance from the attracted point (linear law), the total force of a body on a point is the same as if the whole mass were concentrated at the common center of gravity. Corollary: motion under such a body is equivalent to motion under a spherical mass centered at its center of gravity; orbits are conic with center at the attracting body's center of gravity when that center is at rest or moves uniformly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XC / Prob. XLIV — attraction of a circle on an axis point via area AHIKL
rubrics_metrics.description: Si ad singula circuli cujuscunq; puncta tendant vires centripetæ decrescentes in quacunq; distantiarum ratione: invenire vim qua corpusculum attrahitur ubivis in recta quæ ad planum circuli per centrum ejus perpendicularis consistit. ... erit corpusculi P attractio in circulum ut area AHIKL ducta in altitudinem AP.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Method: construct a curve IKL traced by the perpendiculars to the ordinates proportional to local point-force; the total attraction of the circle on the point on the perpendicular axis equals the area AHIKL divided by the axis length AP. Corollaries: for inverse-square point-laws the area simplifies and the attraction formula reduces to elementary expressions; letting the circle's diameter go to infinity recovers planar results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prop. XCI / Prob. XLV — attraction of a solid on an axial point via section areas
rubrics_metrics.description: In solidum ADEFG trahatur corpusculum P, situm in ejus axe AB. Circulo quolibet RFS ad hunc axem perpendiculari secetur hoc solidum, & in ejus diametro FS ... capiatur longitudo FK vi qua corpusculum P in circulum illum attrahitur proportionalis. ... erit attractio corpusculi P in solidum ut area LABI.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: By slicing the solid with planes perpendicular to the axis and applying the circle-result (Prop. XC) to each slice, the attraction of the whole solid on the axial point reduces to integrating the slice-wise contributions; the resulting total is proportional to a constructed area LABI. Corollaries: special computations for cylinders and spheroids are given (explicit algebraic forms such as AB − PE + PD for a cylinder).
